items.text: Here are four words: dog, big, the, is.
In this order, they do not say anything.
Now put them in the right order.
Now the words give one full idea.
A group of words like this is a sentence.
A sentence begins with a big letter.
And it ends with a full stop.
So it ends with a question mark.
If the words are in the wrong order, it is not a sentence.
The words in a sentence always come in the right order.
Man, house, dog and apple are words that name something.
A word that names a person, an animal, a place or a thing is a noun.
Here is a sentence: the man has a dog.
Man is a noun. Dog is a noun.
Has is not a noun. It does not name anything.
The name of one person or one place is a noun too.
It begins with a big letter: Mary, London.
The cat is in the house.
We say the boy again and again.
In place of the boy, we can say he.
He is a pronoun: a short word we use in place of a noun.
For a man or a boy, we say he.
For a woman or a girl, we say she.
For an animal, we say it.
For a thing, we also say it.
I is the person who is talking.
You is the person you talk to.
We is you and other people together.
They is other people, or other things.
The girl is happy. She is happy.
The dog is small. It is small.
With he, she and it, we use is.
With you, we and they, we use are.
He is, she is, it is.
You are, we are, they are.
We use a before one person or thing.
Apple and egg begin with the sound of a and e. So we use an.
Before the sound of a, e, i, o or u, we use an.
Hour begins with h, but we do not say the h. So: an hour.
University begins with u, but it sounds like you. So: a university.
It is the first sound that matters, not the first letter.
I have a dog and an apple.
For more than one, we add s: cat, cats.
After s, sh, ch and x, we add es: box, boxes.
The plural is the form of a noun for more than one.
Two apples, three boxes, four children.
The children are in the garden.
After am, is and are, we put not.
In talk, we often make is not shorter.
I am not becomes I'm not.
To ask, we put is first: is she a girl?
Now it is a question. It ends with a question mark.
A short answer uses the same word: yes, she is.
With are, it is the same: are goes first.
Am, is and are go first in a question.
Is she a girl? Yes, she is.
Are you a teacher? No, I am not.
Is the dog small? Yes, it is.
Big and small say what the dog is like.
A word that says what a person or a thing is like is an adjective.
An adjective can come before a noun: a big dog.
Or after is: the dog is big.
The adjective does not change. Only the noun gets s.
Happy and tired are adjectives too.
Runs, eats and sits are words for things we do.
A word for something we do, or something that happens, is a verb.
Am, is and are are verbs too.
A verb can change its form to show the time. This is called the tense.
The children play in the garden.
The book is near him, so he says this.
The house is far from him, so he says that.
These is for more than one thing near you.
Those is for more than one thing far from you.
Near you: this for one, these for more than one.
Far from you: that for one, those for more than one.
Look at that house over there.
The dog is new to the man, so she says a dog.
Now he knows about the dog. So she says the dog.
There is only one sun, so we say the sun.
A dog: any dog, a dog that is new to you.
The dog: the one we both know about.
A, an and the are called articles.
I saw a dog. The dog was very big.
She has an apple and a book.
I have a cat. The cat is black.
She eats an egg every day.
The bird is in the sky.
The boy does the action. The boy is the subject.
The ball is what he kicks. The ball is the object.
The cat is the subject. The fish is the object.
Change the order, and the meaning changes.
The subject usually comes before the verb.
The object usually comes after it.
I walk to school every day.
This happens again and again. We use the present simple.
She walks to school every day.
With he, she and it, the verb gets s.
I play. You play. We play. They play.
He plays. She plays. It plays.
After s, sh, ch, x and o, we add es.
The sun rises in the east.
This is always true. We use the present simple for it too.
My father goes to work at eight.
With he, she and it, we use has.
With I, you, we and they, we use have.
I have, you have, we have, they have.
He has, she has, it has.
We also use have for food and for time.
We have a meal at seven.
They have a meal at seven.
The dog has a long tail.
He says do not before the verb.
Put do not before the verb.
With he, she and it, use does not. Then the verb has no s.
When we talk, do not becomes don't.
He does not drive a car. He walks.
He does not drive a car.
We do not have a car.
With he, she and it, use does. Then the verb has no s.
A short answer uses do or does again.
Do you live here? Yes, I do.
Does he work on Sunday? No, he does not.
Does she like music? Yes, she does.
After a verb, I becomes me.
He becomes him. She becomes her.
We becomes us. They becomes them.
You does not change: you see me, I see you.
It does not change: it sees me, I see it.
After to, with and for, we use me, him, her, us and them too.
My says who has the bag.
It: its. We: our. They: their.
Its has no mark in it.
Mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs stand on their own, with no noun after them.
Mary has a cat. It is her cat.
We add 's to girl to show who has the book.
This small mark is called an apostrophe.
Boys ends in s. So we add only the mark: the boys' room.
Children does not end in s.
So we add 's: the children's toys.
The children's toys are on the floor.
Two boys live here. This is the boys' room.
Can and a verb say what someone is able to do.
Can is the same with every subject. The verb after it has no s.
I can not see the sea from here.
We say can not, cannot or can't.
Can you swim? Yes, I can.
To tell someone to do something, begin with the verb.
To tell someone not to do something, use do not.
Do not run in the house.
The ball is in the box.
The ball is on the box.
The cat is under the table.
The book is on the table.
The dog is next to the house.
The girl is between the boys.
The boy is behind the tree.
The girl is in front of the house.
In, on, under and next to are prepositions.
A preposition shows where one thing is, next to another.
The book is on the shelf.
The girl is between the two boys.
At is for a time on the clock.
On is for a day: on Monday, on my birthday.
In is for a month or a year: in May, in this year.
We say in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening.
We play games in the afternoon.
We have a party on my birthday.
These words say how often something happens.
I always drink milk in the morning.
These words come before most verbs.
They come after am, is and are.
He comes at eight every day.
He comes on time every day. He is never late.
We sometimes play in the garden.
It is happening now, at this moment.
Am, is or are, then the verb with ing.
The children are playing in the garden.
But today I am going by car.
Again and again: the present simple.
Now, or for a short time: the present continuous.
Know, like, want and need are about what we think or feel.
We do not use them with ing.
I usually walk to school, but today I am going by car.
Be quiet! The baby is sleeping .
He goes to school every day.
Who is for people. What is for things.
Where is for places. When is for time.
Why asks for a reason. How asks for the way.
The question word comes first. Then comes the rest of the question.
How do you go to school?
How do you go to school?
Where do you live? In London.
Who is that man? He is my father.
When do you get up? At seven.
Why are you sad? Because my dog is ill.
I have a dog and a cat.
I like apples, but I do not like eggs.
Do you want milk or water?
We stayed at home because it was raining.
It was raining, so we stayed at home.
And, but, or, because and so are conjunctions.
A conjunction joins words or parts of a sentence.
I like apples, but I do not like eggs.
I am wearing a coat because it is cold.
It is cold, so I am wearing a coat.
Do you want milk or water?
One apple. Two apples. Three apples.
We can put a number before apple, and it has a plural.
We do not say two waters. Water has no plural.
Apple is countable. Water is uncountable.
Milk, music and money are uncountable too.
Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns.
How many eggs do we have?
We do not have much milk.
How many eggs do we have?
There is a cat in the garden.
There are two cats in the garden.
There is for one. There are for more than one.
There is water in the glass.
With an uncountable noun, use there is too.
There is a book on the table.
Is there a book on the table?
To ask, put is or are first.
There are some birds in the tree.
We say some when we do not say the number.
We do not have any bread.
When we offer something, we use some, even in a question.
I do not have any money.
Was is the past of am and is.
I, he, she and it: was.
Was it cold? Yes, it was.
The past simple is for things that happened and ended before now.
For most verbs, we add ed.
I walked. She walked. They walked.
The past simple is the same with every subject.
She opened the window an hour ago.
Today I go to the shop.
Yesterday I went to the shop.
Some verbs do not add ed. They have their own past form.
She came home and ate an apple.
Take, took. Give, gave. Make, made.
We learn these forms one by one.
I went to the shop yesterday.
Last week we saw a big ship.
Put did first. Then the verb goes back to its simple form.
He did not come to school.
Did not, then the simple form.
Did is the same with every subject.
Did you sleep well? Yes, I did.
I did not go to school.
Did you eat? Yes, I did.
I am going to visit my mother.
This is a plan for the future.
Am, is or are, then going to, then the verb.
Look at the clouds. It is going to rain.
We can see that it will happen.
We are going to play a game after school.
She is not going to come.
We are going to play a game.
Look at the clouds. It is going to rain .
I am not going to swim.
You are not going to cook.
He is not going to sleep.
It is not going to rain.
We are not going to play.
They are not going to help.
We use will and a verb to say what we think will happen.
He chooses to help at that moment, so he says will.
Will is the same with every subject. The verb has no s.
The shop will not open on Sunday.
In talk, will not becomes won't.
This dog is big. That dog is small.
The big dog is bigger than the small dog.
A cow is bigger than a dog.
Some are different: good, better; bad, worse.
My brother is taller than me.
This book is more interesting than that one.
Your bag is better than mine.
This flower is more beautiful than that one.
My house is smaller than yours.
For short adjectives, use the and est.
For long adjectives, use the most.
This is the most beautiful flower.
She is the tallest girl in the class.
This is the best day of my life.
The cow is the biggest animal here.
It is the smallest house here.
Many adverbs are an adjective and ly.
An adverb says more about a verb: how, when or where.
Good is an adjective. Its adverb is well.
The children ran quickly to the door.
How many is for countable nouns.
How much is for uncountable nouns.
We also use how much to ask the price.
How many people are in the room?
How many brothers do you have?
How much water do you drink?
We have to wear a uniform at school.
Must and have to say that something is necessary.
You must not touch the fire.
Must not means it is not allowed.
You do not have to come.
Do not have to means it is not necessary. You can choose.
Do not have to: not necessary.
You must not smoke here. It is not allowed.
You do not have to come. It is your choice.
We have to wear a uniform.
Should says what is a good idea.
Should not: it is not a good idea.
It is late. You should go to bed early.
You should go to bed early.
You should not eat so much sugar.
You are tired. You should go to bed.
It is very cold. You should not go out with no coat.
You should not go to bed.
Was or were, then the verb with ing. This is the past continuous.
We were having a meal at eight.
At eight, the meal was going on.
The long action: I was walking.
The short action that came in the middle: it started to rain.
I was walking home when it started to rain.
We were having a meal at eight.
She was reading when I came.
Each one has a subject and a verb.
A group of words with its own subject and verb is a clause.
She cooks and he cleans the house.
A conjunction joins the two clauses.
I was tired, so I went to bed.
Two subjects, two verbs: two clauses in one sentence.
One subject, one verb: one clause.
I stayed at home because I was ill.
I stayed home because I was ill.
